title: Good and Bad Strategy
hook: A service-ticket printout can expose a fake strategy faster than a polished growth deck.
counterintuition: Ambition can sound decisive and still dodge the hard diagnosis when no obstacle has been named. Good strategy starts with the constraint that governs action.
tryThisNow: Take one active plan and write three lines: the obstacle, the chosen response, and one action you would cut because it does not serve either one.
keyTakeaway: A plan earns the name strategy only when it names the real obstacle, chooses a response, and aligns action tightly enough that scattered effort becomes force.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rebecca sets the service-ticket printout where the laptop was supposed to sit. The repair counter has six fixes proposed, but the printout shows one fact: cracked screens are waiting nine days because parts are scattered across stores. She crosses out the marketing push, the training video, and the new sign. The problem is not energy. The problem is the shape of the work.

Good strategy starts where the real obstacle is named. It names the real obstacle before it rewards action. Bad strategy starts with ambition and then gathers projects around it.

The near-bankrupt company makes the contrast sharp. The company was close to bankruptcy, and the useful move was not a grander speech. The rescue narrowed products, channels, software work, factories, and stock toward survival in personal computers.
breakdown.deepRead:
Apple in September 1997 was not saved by louder ambition; the visible move was a hard narrowing of products, channels, software, factories, and inventory around the problem in front of it. Steve Jobs made the strategy visible by cutting the product maze down until the company could act coherently again. Desktop models went to one. Portable and handheld lines were reduced. Peripherals, retailers, software efforts, manufacturing arrangements, and inventory all faced the same pressure. That matters because the moves were not random cuts. They pointed at one diagnosis: Apple was too complicated for its condition.

A real diagnosis changes the room.

Without it, every action can plead for itself. The repair counter wants a better sign. The store manager wants training. The regional lead wants a promotion. Each suggestion can sound reasonable, which is why bad strategy survives. It lets reasonable pieces sit together without asking what problem should govern them.

Thomas sees the same pattern in a hospital discharge meeting. The nurse callback log shows that weekend patients are returning because medication instructions are being handed off twice, once by a resident and once by a rotating nurse. The room wants a new discharge checklist and a Saturday staffing grid, but the two fixes pull against each other. Thomas points at the callback log and asks which failure they are truly answering before any vote happens.

That is the hard part. A diagnosis does not merely explain. It removes cover. Once the obstacle is named, attractive actions that do not fit start to look expensive, even when their champions still sound sincere.

Good strategy is governed choice. Bad strategy is protected activity.
breakdown.fullRead:
The Microsoft $150 million investment bought Apple time, but money alone did not become the strategy. Time only mattered because the company was being narrowed into a shape that could use it. A cash infusion poured into the old sprawl would have fed the same contradictions. The strategic force came from the fit between diagnosis and action: simplify the line, reduce channels, outsource manufacturing, lower inventory, and stop pretending every product family deserved rescue.

Ask the question in your own setting: what is the condition doing the real damage? Not the embarrassing symptom. Not the public goal. The condition. A team misses release dates because every customer promise is treated as sacred. A clinic misses follow-ups because no one owns the weekend handoff. A library fills the calendar while attendance falls because every program has a defender and no governing audience.

Bad strategy often looks busy because busyness is socially useful. It lets people defend effort without defending fit. A leader can announce alliances, feedback systems, new markets, technical programs, and culture work, then leave the hardest question untouched. What obstacle makes these actions belong together? If no answer appears, the plan may be energetic, but the energy has no center.

Camille learns this after a failed library season. Her program calendar is full, the circulation slips are down, and the locked supply cabinet holds craft materials for six events no one attended. In the postmortem, she stops asking which program needs better promotion. She lays the calendar beside the slips and names the governing problem: too many small events are stealing staff time from the after-school tutoring room that still has a waiting list. The next plan is not more creative. It is more coherent.

There is a limit. Cutting things does not automatically make a strategy good. A retailer can shrink out of fear, a hospital can cancel support that patients need, and a school can drop programs because a budget sheet demands it. Narrowing becomes strategic only when the remaining actions become more mutually reinforcing against the obstacle that matters. If the action gets smaller but no clearer, the organization has only made decline easier to schedule.

That distinction protects the Apple lesson from becoming a worship of cuts. The useful lesson is not smallness. It is coherence under pressure. When the obstacle is sprawl, fewer products and simpler channels can create force. When the obstacle is trust, quality, access, speed, or a missing handoff, the fitting response will look different.

Hugo faces that difference on a SaaS support team. Before the change, every customer complaint became a product promise, every promise became a feature flag, and the refund queue kept growing. After one support transcript is read aloud, he stops the meeting and reorders the work. First: stop promising custom fixes. Second: repair the two failure paths already hurting renewals. Third: tell sales what cannot be sold this quarter. The action feels narrower, but the team finally has a center.

That is what separates good strategy from strategy-shaped busyness. One accepts the pain of choosing. The other keeps every hopeful verb alive and calls the pile momentum.

examples.title: Rebecca Crosses Out the Repair-Counter Extras

planSpec.domain: regional electronics retailer rationalizing repair counters
planSpec.audience: a reader facing regional electronics retailer rationalizing repair counters
planSpec.stakes: whether the next decision produces coherent action or another respectable-looking activity pile
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rebecca moves one concrete constraint to the center of the table and crosses out every action that does not address it using service-ticket printout so the lesson happens as a visible action.

examples.scenario: The service-ticket printout sits where the laptop was supposed to go at the Tuesday regional review. Rebecca, the repair lead, has a cracked phone shell in one hand and an inventory aging report in the other. The table wants six fixes: new signage, longer hours, a training clip, a warranty script, a parts app, and a weekend promo. She has to decide whether to protect the list or cross out every item that does not reduce the nine-day parts delay.
examples.whatToDo: Put the printout at the center, name the parts delay as the governing obstacle, and cut every proposed action that does not shorten that wait.
examples.whyItMatters: The team cannot create force while six answers compete. Once the obstacle is visible, each action can be judged by fit instead of by how responsible it sounds.

examples.title: Thomas Deletes the Extra Weekend Checklist

planSpec.domain: hospital discharge team redesigning weekend handoffs
planSpec.audience: a reader facing hospital discharge team redesigning weekend handoffs
planSpec.stakes: whether the next decision produces coherent action or another respectable-looking activity pile
planSpec.requiredBeat: Thomas asks the room to choose between two incompatible actions, then deletes the weaker one in front of them using discharge checklist so the lesson happens as a visible action.

examples.scenario: "Show me which part this fixes," Thomas says at the Friday discharge huddle, holding up the new checklist beside the nurse callback log. The Saturday staffing grid is open on the charge nurse desk. Two proposals are fighting for the same hour: a second checklist review or one named weekend handoff owner. Thomas must decide before the huddle ends whether to keep both safe-looking actions or delete the weaker one in front of the team.
examples.whatToDo: Force the choice. Keep the named handoff owner if the callback log shows ownership is the failure, and remove the second checklist review from the plan.
examples.whyItMatters: Two plausible fixes can weaken each other when they answer different diagnoses. Choosing one lets weekend staff know what problem they are solving.

examples.title: Camille Finds the Calendar’s Real Drag

planSpec.domain: municipal library cutting a failing program slate
planSpec.audience: a reader facing municipal library cutting a failing program slate
planSpec.stakes: whether the next decision produces coherent action or another respectable-looking activity pile
planSpec.requiredBeat: Camille uses the artifact to expose the hidden constraint before anyone proposes another initiative using program calendar so the lesson happens as a visible action.

examples.scenario: The room smells faintly of toner and rain-soaked coats after the trustees leave. Camille spreads the program calendar beside circulation slips from the past quarter and a photo of the locked supply cabinet. The failed slate looked busy on paper: author nights, craft sessions, coding club, film talks. In the postmortem she marks the hidden constraint in red: every small event stole staff from the tutoring desk families actually used.
examples.whatToDo: Use the calendar and slips to name staff fragmentation as the obstacle, then cut programs that do not support the tutoring demand already visible.
examples.whyItMatters: The old slate failed because activity was mistaken for coherence. The evidence shows which demand should govern the next set of choices.

examples.title: Lukas Marks the One Robotics Path

planSpec.domain: private school robotics club choosing one competition path
planSpec.audience: a reader facing private school robotics club choosing one competition path
planSpec.stakes: whether the next decision produces coherent action or another respectable-looking activity pile
planSpec.requiredBeat: Lukas turns a vague goal into a visible choice by marking the one place effort will land using robotics kit crate so the lesson happens as a visible action.

examples.scenario: You can see the weak spot before anyone names it: three half-built robots, one robotics kit crate, and a competition rule sheet taped to the lab door. "We can enter both divisions," a parent says. Lukas taps the battery tester on the crate. "Then which machine gets the good batteries for the final month?" The club must choose before registration closes whether to chase two trophies or build one reliable machine.
examples.whatToDo: Mark one competition path on the rule sheet and assign the best parts, practice slots, and batteries to that path only.
examples.whyItMatters: A vague goal lets every hope stay alive. A named path makes the scarce parts reinforce one result instead of being spread across two weak entries.

examples.title: Aanya Tests the Import Plan Against Spoilage

planSpec.domain: specialty food importer facing cash and spoiled inventory
planSpec.audience: a reader facing specialty food importer facing cash and spoiled inventory
planSpec.stakes: whether the next decision produces coherent action or another respectable-looking activity pile
planSpec.requiredBeat: Aanya tests the proposed move against the object or record that reveals whether it fits the real problem using customs invoice so the lesson happens as a visible action.

examples.scenario: It took Aanya three weeks to stop trusting the clean version of the plan. The customs invoice looked harmless on her office counter, until a spoiled cheese sample arrived warm and the cash-flow calendar showed two more shipments due before payment cleared. Her sales manager wants a larger order to impress retailers. Aanya has to decide whether to predict demand from interest or test the plan against spoilage and cash first.
examples.whatToDo: Place the invoice, sample, and cash calendar together, then reject any order size that does not solve the delay between customs, shelf life, and payment.
examples.whyItMatters: The real obstacle is not retailer interest. It is the mismatch between cash timing and spoiled inventory, so growth talk only makes the weakness larger.

examples.title: Hugo Reorders the Product-Promise Meeting

planSpec.domain: SaaS support team pruning product promises
planSpec.audience: a reader facing SaaS support team pruning product promises
planSpec.stakes: whether the next decision produces coherent action or another respectable-looking activity pile
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hugo stops the meeting and rearranges the sequence of work so the strategic move becomes visible using support transcript so the lesson happens as a visible action.

examples.scenario: What changes when the constraint is placed in the open? On Monday, Hugo’s SaaS support team starts with a feature flag list and ends with twelve promises nobody owns. On Thursday, he reads one support transcript beside the refund queue and stops the meeting. Before the roadmap review continues, he rearranges the sequence: first stop custom promises, then fix the two failure paths, then tell sales what cannot be sold this quarter.
examples.whatToDo: Lead with the support transcript and refund queue, then reorder the meeting around the failure path instead of the feature list.
examples.whyItMatters: The old meeting protected promises. The new order makes the obstacle govern the work, so product and sales stop adding contradictions.

questions.prompt: A regional gym chain has a plan that lists new classes, a referral drive, lobby paint, instructor training, and a pricing test. Cancellations are rising because evening classes start late. Which response best fits good strategy?
choices: Name late starts as the governing obstacle, then align staffing, room turnover, and class scheduling around fixing that delay.
Keep all five initiatives because each one could improve the member experience in a different way.
Set a more ambitious retention goal so every department feels the urgency of the problem.
questions.explanation: The correct choice names the obstacle and coordinates action around it. Keeping every initiative preserves clutter, while a bigger goal adds pressure without diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A college dining service blames low satisfaction on weak marketing, but comment cards show students leave when the allergen station runs out by noon. What should the director do first?
choices: Launch a campus campaign explaining the quality of the dining program.
Treat the noon allergen shortage as the real obstacle and redirect purchasing, prep, and staff checks toward that station.
Add more menu experiments so students see that the dining team is innovating.
questions.explanation: The station shortage is the obstacle that should govern action. Marketing and menu experiments may sound active, but neither answers the failure students actually feel.

questions.prompt: A repair shop owner wants to respond to slipping margins by buying ads, adding Saturday hours, and launching a loyalty card. The parts shelf shows the same three components are always missing. What is the soundest move?
choices: Buy ads first because more volume will cover the margin problem.
Add the loyalty card first because repeat customers are cheaper to retain.
Use the parts shortage as the diagnosis and coordinate ordering, supplier terms, and technician scheduling around it.
questions.explanation: The missing components explain the margin leak and should shape the response. Ads or loyalty work could increase demand while leaving the core delay untouched.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit board approves a plan with ten priorities after a quiet retreat. The only hard data says donor renewals drop after delayed thank-you calls. What should a new director challenge?
choices: Whether ten priorities are hiding from the renewal obstacle rather than answering it.
Whether the retreat needed more diverse voices before the priorities were approved.
Whether the thank-you call team should use warmer language in its scripts.
questions.explanation: The issue is fit: the priorities do not show how they answer the renewal delay. Broader voices or warmer scripts may help later, but they do not test coherence.

questions.prompt: A city parks team says its strategy is to increase usage, modernize facilities, improve inclusion, build partnerships, and upgrade signage. Weekend field permits are the only service with a waitlist. What is the best critique?
choices: The plan has too few numeric targets to guide accountability.
The plan sounds broad but has not named the obstacle that should organize its choices.
The plan should prioritize partnerships because partners can share the cost burden.
questions.explanation: The critique is that the plan has no governing problem. Numeric targets and partners can be useful, but they do not substitute for a diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A medical device startup says it will win through bold culture, fast hiring, international expansion, and constant customer listening. Lab notes show sterilization failures are delaying every pilot. Which option shows coherent action?
choices: Pause expansion hiring, assign engineering to sterilization reliability, and make pilots depend on passing that test.
Keep hiring fast because more engineers will eventually solve the sterilization issue.
Begin international expansion early so one market delay does not stop the company.
questions.explanation: This action lets the sterilization obstacle govern hiring and pilots. The other choices add motion while the one failure controlling progress remains unresolved.

questions.prompt: A school principal inherits a plan full of slogans about excellence and belonging. Attendance records show ninth graders miss the first period after late bus arrivals. What would make the plan strategic?
choices: Replacing the slogans with a shorter inspirational statement that staff can remember.
Building a coordinated response around buses, first-period scheduling, family contact, and ninth-grade monitoring.
Creating a committee to collect more values from teachers and families.
questions.explanation: The coordinated response fits the actual attendance obstacle. A better slogan or broader values process may feel inclusive, but neither organizes action around the cause.

questions.prompt: A bakery cuts its wholesale line after seeing that retail customers spend more per order. Two months later, staff have fewer shifts and retail still misses daily targets because morning production is late. How should you evaluate the cut?
choices: It was strategic because cutting any line creates focus.
It was strategic because retail has a higher average order value.
It was not yet strategic because the cut did not address the production delay that controlled retail performance.
questions.explanation: Narrowing counts only when it improves coherence around the real obstacle. Higher order value and fewer lines do not matter if late production still controls results.

questions.prompt: A software team has three proposals after churn rises: add onboarding videos, discount annual plans, and hire customer success reps. Exit interviews show customers leave after one broken data import. What should guide the choice?
choices: Which proposal is fastest to announce to customers.
Which proposal best coordinates product, support, and sales around fixing the import failure.
Which proposal is cheapest this quarter.
questions.explanation: The import failure is the obstacle that should organize the response across functions. Speed and cost matter, but they are secondary if the action misses the reason customers leave.

reviewCards.front: A plan has many energetic initiatives but no named obstacle. What should you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Ask what problem governs the plan. If no single obstacle explains why the actions belong together, the plan is still activity, not coherent strategy.

reviewCards.front: A leader proposes cutting three projects. What condition makes the cut strategic instead of mere retreat?
reviewCards.back: The cut must make the remaining actions reinforce one another against the real obstacle. Smaller is not enough; clearer and more coherent is the test.

reviewCards.front: Your team wants to protect every popular action in a turnaround plan. What is the retrieval move?
reviewCards.back: Name the diagnosis, then test each action against it. Actions that do not answer the diagnosis lose protection, even if they sound responsible.

reviewCards.front: Why can a polished list of alliances, systems, and market pushes still be bad strategy?
reviewCards.back: Because the list may never name the obstacle that makes the actions fit. Strategy needs a governing problem and coordinated response, not just serious nouns.

reviewCards.front: What does Apple in 1997 help you remember about strategy under pressure?
reviewCards.back: The useful lesson is coherence. Jobs narrowed products, channels, software work, manufacturing, and inventory around the problem of sprawl, so the actions added force.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning plans into governed choices. Name the obstacle first, choose the response second, and let actions survive only if they reinforce that response.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a planning meeting starts collecting initiatives, then write the suspected obstacle at the top of the page and ask which actions would still matter if that obstacle ruled the decision.
If an action sounds popular but does not fit the diagnosis, then mark it as deferred instead of letting it stay on the plan as a protected extra.
If a group project has too many deliverables, then choose the one failure that would sink the grade and align roles around preventing it.
If your own plan keeps expanding, then name the bottleneck and remove one task that creates motion without reducing it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, take one plan you can influence and rewrite it as three bullets: obstacle, chosen response, coherent action. Remove one action that does not fit.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit a live plan for clutter. Circle the governing obstacle, underline the actions that directly answer it, and move the rest to a separate parking list.

memorableLines.text: Good strategy starts where the real obstacle is named.
memorableLines.why: A short landing line turns the service-ticket scene into a clean rule.

memorableLines.text: A real diagnosis changes the room.
memorableLines.why: The line makes diagnosis feel like an event, not a planning term.
The sentence compresses the chapter move into a phrase the reader can retrieve.
